message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code and related laws. Here’s an overview of your key rights (and some obligations) as a renter: | Category | What You’re Entitled To | How It Works | |----------|------------------------|--------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for residential units; two months for furnished units.
• Must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear. | • Landlord must give a written itemized list of deductions if they keep any portion. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain the premises in a safe, livable condition—plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, pest control, etc. | • If repairs aren’t made promptly, you can withhold rent, repair & deduct, or file a complaint with local health/inspections. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlord cannot enter without notice (usually 24‑hour written notice unless emergency). | • Exceptions: emergencies, repairs, inspections, showing unit to prospective renters/buyers. | | **Notice Requirements** | • For non‑renewal or termination: 90 days’ notice for month‑to‑month leases; 30 days for fixed‑term leases ending. | • Written notice required; must specify reason if lease requires it. | | **Rent Increases** | • No limit on how much or how often you can increase rent, but must comply with lease terms and give proper notice (typically 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Some cities have local rent‑control ordinances—check city ordinances if applicable. | | **Discrimination Protections** | • Protected against discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, source of income, etc. | • Fair Housing Act applies at federal level; Texas law adds protection for LGBTQ+ individuals. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow formal eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment), file a lawsuit, obtain a judgment, then sheriff’s execution. | • You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If landlord fails to fix major problems, you may repair them yourself and deduct cost from rent (up to $500 per year). | • Must notify landlord in writing before making repairs. | | **Lease Termination** | • You can terminate early if landlord breaches habitability standards or fails to provide required notices. | • Provide written notice and document the breach. | | **Privacy Rights** | • Landlord must respect your privacy; no unlawful searches or surveillance. | • Landlord may conduct reasonable inspections but must give notice. | ### Practical Steps If Issues Arise 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, photos of damage, receipts for repairs, etc. 2. **Written Notice** – Always send notices via certified mail or email with read receipt to establish proof. 3. **Local Resources** – Contact your county or city housing department, or the Texas Attorney General’s Office for consumer complaints. 4. **Legal Aid** – If you need representation, look for nonprofit legal aid organizations in your area. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist - [ ] Lease signed? - [ ] Security deposit returned? - [ ] Repairs done? - [ ] Proper notice given? - [ ] Discrimination complaint filed? If you’d like a sample lease template or a more detailed guide tailored to your situation, let me know!
